En 1735, il fait imprimer aux Pays-Bas l: In 1735, he had the first edition of his Systema Naturae printed in the Netherlands, a twelve-page work that sorted the three kingdoms of nature. The following editions kept growing.
Systema Naturae, 1735 : douze pages au d: Systema Naturae, 1735: twelve pages to begin with.
Linné donne à chaque espèce un nom en de: Linnaeus gave each species a two-word name, genus then species, like Homo sapiens. His Species Plantarum, in 1753, is accepted worldwide as the starting point for plant names.
Pour les animaux, le point de départ est: For animals, the starting point is the 10th edition of Systema Naturae, in 1758. An older name, however well chosen, does not count.
Plantes : 1753. Animaux : 1758. Avant, ç: Plants: 1753. Animals: 1758. Before that, it doesn't count.
Professeur à Uppsala, Linné appelle 17 d: A professor at Uppsala, Linnaeus called 17 of his students his "apostles" and sent them to collect plants on every continent. In 1761, he was ennobled and became Carl von Linné. His favourite plant, a small woodland flower, bears his name: Linnaea borealis.
Il meurt le 10 janvier 1778. En 1959, le: He died on 10 January 1778. In 1959, the botanist William Stearn designated him as the type specimen of Homo sapiens: he is the only human Linnaeus is known to have examined.
17 apôtres, un titre de noblesse, et Lin: 17 apostles, a noble title, and Linnaeus a specimen of his own species.
Douze marins, six remèdes, deux oranges: Twelve sailors, six remedies, two oranges; an eight-year-old boy and a cow called Blossom. The 18th century learned to test.

Le 20 mai 1747, sur le Salisbury, James: On 20 May 1747, aboard the Salisbury, James Lind split 12 sailors with scurvy between 6 treatments: only the citrus works.
Son Traité du scorbut, en 1753, est pres: His Treatise of the Scurvy, in 1753, was mostly ignored; the Royal Navy only issued lemon juice to the whole fleet after his death.

Jenner publie son Inquiry en 1798 ; l'OM: Jenner published his Inquiry in 1798; the WHO declared smallpox eradicated in 1980.

James Lind naît à Édimbourg le 4 octobre: James Lind was born in Edinburgh on 4 October 1716. A naval surgeon, on 20 May 1747, aboard HMS Salisbury patrolling the Bay of Biscay, he began a trial on twelve sailors with scurvy, split two by two.
Chaque paire reçoit un traitement : du c: Each pair received one treatment: cider, elixir of vitriol, vinegar, seawater, two oranges and a lemon, or a spicy paste. The citrus eaters recovered. It is one of the first controlled clinical trials.
En 1753, Lind publie son Traité du scorb: In 1753, Lind published his Treatise of the Scurvy, which was mostly ignored. And he himself never presented citrus as the single remedy: he believed scurvy had several causes.
Médecin-chef de l'hôpital naval de Hasla: Chief physician of the Haslar naval hospital from 1758, he died on 13 July 1794. The following year, the Admiralty agreed to issue lemon juice to the whole fleet.
The right result, ignored for forty years.
Contre la variole, on pratique déjà la v: Against smallpox, variolation was already practised: in 1721, Lady Mary Wortley Montagu imported it from Constantinople to Britain. And in 1774, the farmer Benjamin Jesty inoculated his wife and two children with cowpox, a mild disease of cows.
Le 14 mai 1796, Edward Jenner prélève du: On 14 May 1796, Edward Jenner took pus from a milkmaid, Sarah Nelmes, infected by a cow called Blossom, and inoculated it into James Phipps, aged 8, his gardener's son. His first paper was not published; he published his Inquiry in 1798. In 1980, the WHO declared smallpox eradicated.
Jenner, 1796 : de Blossom à Phipps ; var: Jenner, 1796: from Blossom to Phipps; smallpox eradicated in 1980.
Au XIXe siècle, Semmelweis et Snow compt: In the 19th century, Semmelweis and Snow counted the dead to find causes: hypothesis, control group, falsifiability.
En 1859, L'Origine des espèces : sélecti: In 1859, On the Origin of Species: natural selection, mutations, and the whole history of life.
Des pois de Mendel à la double hélice :: From Mendel's peas to the double helix: genes, alleles, heredity, DNA and mutations.
Bactéries, virus, vaccins, antibiotiques: Bacteria, viruses, vaccines, antibiotics: the late 19th century identified microbes, the 20th fought them.
Le mot naît avec Haeckel ; Rachel Carson: The word was born with Haeckel; Rachel Carson raised the alarm: food chains, cycles, biodiversity and climate.
De Dolly à CRISPR : ADN recombinant, PCR: From Dolly to CRISPR: recombinant DNA, PCR, cloning and RNA vaccines.
